content: Ascaris lumbricoides is one of several species of Ascaris and is classified as an ascarid nematode within the phylum Nematoda. It is the largest and most common parasitic worm infecting humans. This organism is responsible for causing ascariasis, a type of helminthiasis and one of the neglected tropical diseases. Approximately one-sixth of the global human population is infected with A. lumbricoides or another roundworm species. Ascariasis is prevalent worldwide, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions. Life Cycle The life cycle of A. lumbricoides begins when a fertilized egg is ingested by a human host. The egg hatches into a larval worm in the duodenum, where it penetrates the intestinal wall and enters the bloodstream. From there, it is transported to the liver and heart, eventually reaching the pulmonary circulation. The larvae break free into the alveoli of the lungs, where they grow and molt. After approximately three weeks, the larvae migrate from the respiratory system to the pharynx, where they are coughed up and swallowed, returning to the small intestine. In the small intestine, the larvae mature into adult male or female worms. Fertilization occurs, and female worms can produce up to 200,000 eggs per day for a year. These fertilized eggs become infectious after two weeks in soil and can persist in the environment for over 10 years due to their lipid layer, which provides resistance to acids, alkalis, and other chemicals. This resilience contributes to the widespread nature of this parasite. Morphology A. lumbricoides is notable for its large size. Male worms have a ventrally curved posterior end with a bluntly pointed tail, while females are wider and longer. The vulva of the female is located in the anterior third of the body. The uterus of a female worm can contain up to 27 million eggs at a time, with 200,000 eggs being laid daily. Fertilized eggs are oval to round in shape, with a thick outer shell, while unfertilized eggs are elongated and narrower. Epidemiology More than 2 billion people worldwide are affected by A. lumbricoides infections. The eggs of this parasite are highly resistant to strong chemicals, desiccation, and low temperatures, allowing them to remain viable in soil for months or even years. Eggs have been identified in archaeological coprolites from various regions, including the Americas, Europe, Africa, the Middle East, and New Zealand, with some dating back over 24,000 years. Infections Infections are more common in areas with poor sanitation, particularly where raw human feces are used as fertilizer. The eggs, which are too small to be seen with the naked eye, can contaminate food and water. They may adhere to vegetables when improperly treated human feces are used as fertilizer. Infection can also occur through handling food without proper hygiene, as eggs can remain on hands, clothing, hair, raw produce, or even cooked food that has been re-contaminated. Bleach does not readily kill A. lumbricoides eggs but can remove their sticky coating, allowing them to be rinsed away. Hot composting methods can reduce the number of eggs, but complete eradication may require extreme measures such as high heat, rubbing alcohol, iodine, or specialized chemicals. Symptoms In many cases, A. lumbricoides infections are asymptomatic. However, in severe infections, symptoms may include bloody sputum, cough, fever, abdominal discomfort, intestinal ulcers, and the passage of worms. Ascariasis is the most common cause of Löffler's syndrome globally, which is characterized by pulmonary infiltration, eosinophilia, and radiographic opacities. Prevention Preventing fecal-borne diseases like ascariasis requires proper hygiene practices and effective fecal treatment systems. This is particularly important for A. lumbricoides, as its eggs are among the most resilient pathogens, second only to prions. The eggs can survive in the environment for 1–3 years. Preventive measures include avoiding the use of untreated human feces as fertilizer, thoroughly washing vegetables, and ensuring proper food handling practices. Details of Infection Process Infections occur when humans ingest water or food contaminated with unhatched eggs. The eggs hatch into juveniles in the duodenum, where they penetrate the mucosa and submucosa, entering venules or lymphatics. The juveniles then pass through the right heart and into the pulmonary circulation, breaking out of the capillaries to enter the air spaces of the lungs. Acute tissue reactions may occur when worms become lost during migration and accumulate in other organs. The juveniles migrate from the lungs up the respiratory tract to the pharynx, where they are swallowed. They begin producing eggs within 60–65 days of being swallowed. These eggs are produced in the small intestine, where the juveniles mature. The migration process may mimic an intermediate host, which could have been required for ancestral forms of the parasite to develop to the third stage. Alternatively, tissue migration may enable faster growth and larger size, increasing reproductive capacity. Diagnosis and Treatment Diagnosis is typically made by identifying the presence of worms or eggs in feces. Due to the large number of eggs laid, diagnosis can often be achieved with just one or two fecal smears. Infections are treated with drugs known as ascaricides. The treatment of choice is mebendazole, which works by binding to tubulin in the worms' intestinal cells and body-wall muscles. Other effective drugs include nitazoxanide and ivermectin.
